title: Split into Chunks with yield
oneLiner: Write a lazy iterator that cuts any sequence, even an endless one, into lists of a given size.
keyTakeaway: Collect items into a small buffer and yield it each time it fills, then yield whatever is left at the end. Because nothing is read ahead, the same code works on a list, a file or an endless sequence, using memory for one chunk at a time.
explanation:
Write Chunks(items, size), which yields the items in lists of size items each, in order; the last chunk may be shorter. Chunks([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2) yields [1, 2], [3, 4] and then [5]. An empty input yields nothing. size is at least 1.

The input is any sequence, IEnumerable<int> in C# and any iterable in Python, and it may never end: one test passes the endless sequence 1, 2, 3, ... and takes just the first few chunks. So you can't ask for its length, index into it, slice it, or turn it into a list first (that would never finish). Loop over it once with foreach / for.

Keep a list for the current chunk. Add each item; when the chunk reaches size, yield it and start a new list (in C#, a new List<int>, not Clear() on the old one, which the caller already holds). After the loop, yield the last chunk if it isn't empty. The C# method returns IEnumerable<List<int>> and uses yield return; the Python function uses yield. The tests show the chunks as a list of lists, with an endlessChunks argument saying how many chunks to take from the endless sequence (0 means use the given items).

visualizationSteps.message: Chunks of 2. The current chunk starts empty.
The chunk is full: yield it. The caller gets [1, 2] now, before 3 is even read.
The chunk is full: yield it. The caller gets [3, 4] now, before 5 is even read.
The input ran out with [5] left over: yield it as the last, shorter chunk.

complexity.note: Every item is touched once. The iterator holds only the current chunk of k items, which is why it works on an endless input; collecting all the chunks into a list, as the tests do, is O(n) more.
